c.tagline: Ancient Aztec roots beneath vibrant sprawling metropolis.

emergency.note: 911 is the single nationwide emergency number; English-speaking operators are limited, and Locatel (55 5658 1111) offers city assistance.

hood_landmark.Condesa: Parque México's leafy Art Deco promenades
hood_landmark.Roma: Plaza Río de Janeiro with its David replica and café-lined Álvaro Obregón
hood_landmark.Centro Historico: the Zócalo plaza and Metropolitan Cathedral

avoid.reason: Avoid Tepito and the Doctores neighbourhood — high street crime.
Caution in the historic centre after dark and in Iztapalapa; use registered taxis/rideshare, not street cabs.

hood_desc: Condesa is a leafy, bohemian-chic district of Art Deco buildings, tree-lined avenues and buzzing sidewalk cafes and bars, ideal for younger travelers and digital nomads who want walkable nightlife and green parks.

Roma is a stylish, artsy neighborhood of restored mansions, indie galleries, specialty coffee and acclaimed restaurants, suiting foodies and creatives who want hip energy with a slightly more grown-up edge than Condesa.

Polanco is Mexico City's upscale, polished quarter of luxury hotels, designer boutiques on Avenida Presidente Masaryk and fine dining, best for affluent travelers and business visitors wanting comfort and safety.

Coyoacan is a charming, historic colonial village with cobblestone streets, plazas, markets and the Frida Kahlo house, appealing to culture lovers and families who prefer a slower, bohemian and authentically Mexican atmosphere.

Centro Historico is the dense, monumental old core around the Zocalo, packed with cathedrals, museums, ruins and street life, perfect for first-time visitors and history buffs who want to be steps from the main sights.

water.note: Avoid tap water; drink bottled or purified water, and confirm ice is made from purified water.

transit.pay: You need the rechargeable MI (Movilidad Integrada) card - paper tickets were discontinued in 2024. It costs MXN 15 (~US$0.80) plus fare balance, sold at metro station ticket booths (cash) and Metrobus/Cablebus vending machines, and works across the metro, Metrobus, Cablebus, light rail and trolleybuses. Rides are cheap: Metro MXN 5 (~US$0.25), Metrobus MXN 6.
transit.hours: Metro runs 5am-midnight weekdays, from 6am Saturdays and 7am Sundays/holidays; Metrobus Line 1 runs nearly 24 hours but most lines stop around midnight.

landmarks: Zócalo (Plaza de la Constitución)
Mexico City's monumental central plaza, one of the largest public squares in the world, framed by the Cathedral and National Palace.
Metropolitan Cathedral
The largest cathedral in the Americas, its ornate baroque facade dominates the Zócalo skyline.
Palacio de Bellas Artes
A stunning white-marble Art Nouveau/Art Deco palace topped with a colorful mosaic dome, iconic against Mexico City's skyline.
Chapultepec Castle
A hilltop royal castle offering sweeping panoramic views over Chapultepec Park and the city.
Angel of Independence
A gleaming gold-winged victory column on Paseo de la Reforma, the city's most recognizable monument.
Teotihuacán (Pyramid of the Sun)
Ancient pre-Aztec pyramids just outside the city, spectacular for sunrise hot-air-balloon photos.
Frida Kahlo Museum (Casa Azul)
The vivid cobalt-blue house where Frida Kahlo lived, filled with her art and personal belongings.
Torre Latinoamericana
A historic skyscraper with an observation deck delivering the best 360-degree views of the Centro Histórico.
Xochimilco
Colorful gondola-like trajinera boats gliding through Aztec-era canals, a lively and photogenic UNESCO site.
Basílica of Our Lady of Guadalupe
Mexico's most important pilgrimage site, with a modern circular basilica beside the historic tilted old church.

train.note: Mexico has no international passenger trains and no intercity rail network from the capital. The much-publicised Tren Maya (trenmaya.gob.mx) is a regional line in the Yucatán, over 1,000 km away; the only passenger train from Mexico City itself is the El Insurgente commuter line to Toluca. For long-distance travel use buses or flights.

bus.note: No reliable direct international coaches leave Mexico City: for Guatemala, take a domestic overnight bus to Tapachula and continue with Tica Bus (https://www.ticabus.com/en/), and tickets sold towards Texas usually involve a change at Monterrey or the border. Main long-distance domestic operators are ADO (https://www.ado.com.mx/) from TAPO/Terminal Norte and ETN (https://etn.com.mx/).

ferry.note: Mexico City sits inland at 2,240 m — there are no ferries. Mexico's main passenger ferries (Baja Ferries, between Baja California and the mainland) sail from ports hundreds of kilometres away.

half.name: Puebla

half.name: Tepoztlán

half.name: Cuernavaca
half.blurb: Known as the city of eternal spring for its warm climate, gardens and colonial palace.

half.name: Tula
half.blurb: People come to see the towering stone Atlante warrior statues of this ancient Toltec capital.

full.name: Valle de Bravo
